title: Women’s basketball draws record crowds. Its players need room to recover, too
subtitle: FIBA’s promise to end back-to-back World Cup games in 2030 puts working conditions alongside commercial growth—but a better calendar remains a commitment to deliver.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: FIBA has promised that the 2030 Women’s Basketball World Cup in Tokyo will avoid back-to-back games, after its secretary general, Andreas Zagklis, acknowledged problems with Berlin’s compressed schedule. His comments came on 13 September and were reported by Reuters on 15 September. The WNBA resumes on 17 September, four days after the final. A league spokesperson welcomed calendar coordination that helps players meet club and international commitments.

That is a significant promise in a sport whose growing audience is increasingly measurable. FIBA reports 236,015 attendances across Berlin’s 36 games, compared with 145,519 across 38 games in Sydney in 2022. These are cumulative attendances, not a count of unique people, and the governing body—not an independent auditor—is the source. Even with those qualifications, the figures document a larger audience inside the arenas.
What is new—and what was already decided

The move to a later World Cup is not a decision made this week. FIBA approved a November–December window in May 2025. Its April 2026 calendar update lists the Tokyo tournament for 26 November to 8 December 2030. The fresh development is the explicit assurance about avoiding games on consecutive days.

Separating those decisions matters. Moving a tournament can reduce one scheduling collision; it does not automatically establish adequate rest across a player’s entire year. Travel, preparation and other competition commitments still need to fit around the dates.

FIBA’s own Women In Basketball Forum in Berlin shows the breadth of interests involved. Sue Bird discussed athletes’ expanding roles beyond playing, while New York Liberty owner Clara Wu Tsai participated in a session on investment. Broadcasters and sponsors also featured in discussions about the sport’s future. This was the organiser’s account of its forum, rather than evidence that every participant agreed on scheduling reforms.

The commercial opportunity is real, but the question for players is how its benefits are distributed. More valuable competitions should create space for athletes to negotiate sustainable workloads, not merely more obligations to fulfil.

The next test will be the published match schedule and the recovery time it actually protects. Crowds measure demand for women’s basketball. The calendar will help show how seriously its institutions value the women producing it.
